units.title: Querying with SQL
units.description: Learn the declarative power of SQL to extract insights from data, moving from simple filters to complex multi-table joins and analytical aggregations.

lectures.title: Retrieving Data
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the core syntax of SQL data retrieval, focusing on selecting, filtering, and ordering data to build the foundation for complex query construction.

sessions.title: SELECT and FROM
sessions.description: This session covers the basic projection and selection mechanism of SQL, teaching you how to specify which columns you want and which table they reside in. By the end of this session, you will be able to write your first syntactically correct SQL queries to view raw data. Understanding these keywords is your first step toward transforming large datasets into manageable views.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by establishing the 'Mental Model of Retrieval.' Before writing a single line of code, the instructor should draw a massive, messy filing cabinet on the whiteboard to represent a database. The goal is to introduce the SELECT and FROM keywords not as arbitrary commands, but as a lens that focuses our attention. We explain that in a world of massive data, the most critical skill is not just having the information, but isolating exactly what we need. By framing SELECT as 'what do you want to see?' and FROM as 'where is it located?', we give the learner a spatial framework for understanding the relational model.

The instructor should then pivot to the syntax of the 'SELECT *' wildcard. It is crucial to present this as the 'I'm feeling lucky' button of SQL—useful for exploration but dangerous in production environments. On the whiteboard, visualize this as dumping the entire contents of a table onto a screen. While explaining the 'Users' table example, the instructor should highlight a common pitfall: assuming the order of columns in a '*' query is guaranteed. We explain that relying on '*' can break backend applications if the underlying schema changes, planting the seed for 'defensive coding' early in their database journey.

Next, we transition to the concept of 'Projection'—the precise act of selecting specific columns like 'username' and 'email'. This is the session's 'Aha!' moment. The instructor should contrast the heavy, slow 'SELECT *' with the surgical precision of naming columns. Draw a table with ten columns, then draw a narrow 'view' or vertical slice that only captures two. Explain that this isn't just about clean UI; it’s about performance and network efficiency. In backend engineering, fetching only what you need saves memory and bandwidth. This prepares the learner for the practice task of narrowing down a 'Users' table to just identity markers.

To close, we address the 'Invisible Traps' of syntax. The instructor should demonstrate that SQL is generally case-insensitive but convention-heavy, recommending uppercase for keywords to make the 'logic' pop out from the 'data'. A key pedagogical move here is to purposely omit the comma between column names or forget the table name to show how the database engine 'complains.' By interpreting these errors for the student, we lower the barrier to entry. We then move into the practice block, where the student writes their first query. The task of selecting 'username' and 'email' is designed to test if they understand the comma as a separator and the concept that columns can be reordered in the SELECT clause regardless of how they are stored on disk.

tasks: Write a query to select all columns from a 'Users' table.
Write a query to select only the 'username' and 'email' columns from the 'Users' table.

sessions.title: Filtering with WHERE
sessions.description: This session explores the WHERE clause, which allows you to apply logical conditions to filter rows returned by a query. You will learn how to use comparison operators and logical connectors like AND/OR to pinpoint specific records. This skill is essential for backend engineering tasks such as finding a specific user profile or identifying products within a price range.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the 'what' of the last session—selecting columns—to the 'which' of data retrieval. I start by drawing a massive table on the whiteboard filled with hundreds of rows of generic user data. I'll point out that while SELECT defines the vertical slice of our data, the WHERE clause is our horizontal scalpel. The core intuition to establish here is that the WHERE clause acts as a 'gatekeeper' for every single row in a table. I want students to visualize the database engine scanning the table row-by-row, asking a simple Yes/No question: 'Does this row satisfy my condition?' If yes, it passes through the gate; if no, it is discarded from the result set.

To build the syntax, I’ll write a simple comparison like 'price > 100' on the board. I'll explain that this isn't just math; it’s a predicate. I’ll introduce the standard toolkit of comparison operators (=, <>, <, >, <=, >=), specifically highlighting the SQL-specific diamond operator (<>) for 'not equal,' as this often trips up those coming from C-style programming backgrounds. I’ll use a product catalog example to show how these operators work with numbers, but quickly pivot to strings—showing how 'status = 'Active'' requires single quotes. This is a common point of failure for beginners, so I will emphasize that strings are literal data while column names are structural identifiers.

Next, we move into the logic of combination using AND and OR. This is where most logical errors occur. I’ll draw a Venn diagram to visualize how 'AND' narrows our search (the intersection) while 'OR' expands it (the union). To illustrate the danger of ambiguity, I’ll write a query like 'category = 'Electronics' OR category = 'Books' AND price < 50' and ask the students what they think it does. This leads into a crucial discussion on operator precedence—how AND is evaluated before OR. I will teach them to 'defend their logic' by always using parentheses to wrap conditions, ensuring the query behaves exactly as their mental model intended.

The first practice task involves filtering a products table for prices greater than 100. This is a baseline check to ensure they understand the basic syntax and data types. The second task, retrieving orders after a specific date that are 'Pending,' is more diagnostic; it tests their ability to handle dates as strings or special types and their comfort with combining multiple criteria using AND. I’ll watch for students who forget the single quotes around the date or the status string.

Finally, I will conclude by addressing the 'implicit filter' concept. I want them to understand that a query without a WHERE clause is effectively saying 'WHERE True' for every row. By framing it this way, we prepare them for more advanced logical concepts later in the course, such as JOIN conditions and subqueries. We'll end the session by 'dry-running' a complex filter on our whiteboard table, physically crossing out rows that fail the AND/OR logic to solidify the concept of row-level elimination before we move on to sorting the complexities of NULL values.

tasks: Filter a products table for items with a price greater than 100.
Retrieve orders that were placed after a specific date and are currently 'Pending'.

sessions.title: Sorting and Limiting Results
sessions.description: In this session, you will learn to organize your query output using ORDER BY and restrict the volume of data using LIMIT. You will gain the ability to rank data and implement pagination logic. Mastering these clauses is vital for building performant applications that don't overwhelm the user or the network with excessive data.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by acknowledging that while we can now retrieve specific data using SELECT and WHERE, the order of that data currently feels random—it is essentially 'whatever the database engine found first.' This is the perfect moment to introduce the concept of 'Presentation Logic' vs. 'Storage Logic.' We explain that in the relational model, tables are unordered sets. If you want order, you must explicitly ask for it. This sets the stage for the ORDER BY clause, the primary tool for bringing predictable structure to our result sets.

I will illustrate the syntax of ORDER BY by returning to our employee table example. The key insight to convey is that sorting is rarely just about alphabetical names; it’s about hierarchy and chronology. I'll demonstrate sorting by 'Hire Date' to show how the database handles temporal data. This is where I introduce the ASC (Ascending) and DESC (Descending) keywords. A common trap for learners is assuming the database remembers the last sort order used; I need to emphasize that order is ephemeral and must be defined in every single query where it matters.

Next, we tackle the 'Top-N' problem. Why pull ten thousand records if you only need the five highest-paid employees? This leads naturally into the LIMIT clause (or TOP/FETCH depending on the dialect, though we will stick to the standard LIMIT for this concept-first lecture). I’ll use a whiteboard diagram to show the flow of data: first, the database identifies all matching rows (WHERE), then it sorts them (ORDER BY), and only then does it 'cut off' the stream at the number specified by LIMIT. Visualizing this sequence is crucial for understanding performance—sorting a million rows just to see the top five still requires the database to process those million rows first.

To solidify this, we will engage in a practice task: identifying the top 5 most expensive products. I will ask the students to consider what happens if they forget the ORDER BY and only use LIMIT 5. This 'negative example' reveals the danger: they get 5 random products, not the most expensive ones. This exercise highlights that LIMIT and ORDER BY are almost always inseparable partners in professional backend development.

Finally, I will briefly touch upon the operational reality of pagination. In modern web apps, we don't load all results at once; we load 'Page 1,' then 'Page 2.' I will introduce the OFFSET keyword as the companion to LIMIT. I’ll draw a 'window' sliding over a long list of data to show how `LIMIT 10 OFFSET 20` skips the first two pages to show the third. I’ll warn the students about the performance cost of high offsets—how the database still has to 'count' the skipped rows—preparing them for the deeper performance discussions in Unit 4.

tasks: Sort a list of employees by their hire date in descending order.
Retrieve the top 5 most expensive products from a catalog.

sessions.title: NULL and Three-Valued Logic
sessions.description: This session demystifies the concept of NULL as a marker for missing data and how it impacts logic via the Three-Valued Logic (True, False, Unknown) system. You will understand why standard comparisons fail with NULL and how to use IS NULL correctly. This knowledge prevents subtle bugs in data reporting and application logic when dealing with optional data fields.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by confronting one of the most persistent sources of bugs in database engineering: the concept of nothingness. In SQL, NULL is not a zero, an empty string, or a space; it is a marker for 'unknown' or 'missing' information. I will start the whiteboard by drawing a table of users where some have phone numbers and others have empty cells. The key intuition to land here is that NULL is a state, not a value. If I ask, 'Is this unknown value equal to 5?', the answer cannot be 'Yes' or 'No'—it must be 'I don't know.' This transition from binary logic to Three-Valued Logic (3VL) is the foundational shift students must make to master data integrity.

To visualize Three-Valued Logic, I will draw a truth table for AND, OR, and NOT, but with a third column labeled 'Unknown.' We will walk through scenarios: What is 'True AND Unknown'? What is 'False AND Unknown'? I'll explain that 'False' usually wins in an AND because one false part ruins the whole, but 'Unknown' propagates when the outcome depends on the missing data. This is critical because SQL's WHERE clause only keeps rows where the condition evaluates to 'True.' If a condition evaluates to 'Unknown,' the row is discarded just as if it were 'False.' This 'silent failure' is why many developers miss records they intended to include.

Next, I will demonstrate the failure of standard operators. I'll write 'WHERE phone = NULL' on the board and then cross it out with a large red 'X.' I will explain that since NULL is unknown, comparing anything to it results in 'Unknown.' To interact with these markers, we must use the specific predicates 'IS NULL' and 'IS NOT NULL.' I'll frame these as identity checks rather than value comparisons. This is a perfect moment for a practice task: asking students to find users without phone numbers. If they try to use the equals sign, I'll use that mistake to reinforce that the database is effectively saying, 'I don't know if this missing value is equal to that missing value.'

Finally, we will explore the 'NOT IN' trap, which is a classic senior-level interview question. I'll present a scenario where we want to find products not in a specific list, but that list contains a NULL. I will show how the entire query returns zero results because 'NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)' expands to 'val != 1 AND val != 2 AND val != NULL.' Since the last part is always 'Unknown,' the entire expression can never be 'True.' This illustrates the operational danger of NULLs in complex logic. I will conclude by teaching students that while NULLs are necessary for flexible schemas, they require defensive query writing and a solid grasp of how 'Unknown' ripples through their logic.

tasks: Write a query to find users who have not provided a phone number.
Predict the output of a WHERE clause involving NULL comparisons.

lectures.title: Combining Tables
lectures.description: This lecture explores the power of the relational model by teaching you how to stitch disparate tables together using various JOIN techniques and set operations.

sessions.title: Inner Joins
sessions.description: This session introduces the Inner Join, the most common method of combining tables based on matching values in related columns. You will learn to use visual Venn diagrams to understand how rows from two tables are paired. This is the core mechanism for resolving the junction tables and relationships you designed in the previous unit.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing the fundamental 'problem' of the relational model: we split data into multiple tables to avoid redundancy, but our users want that data back in a single view. I will start the whiteboard session by drawing two isolated boxes—an 'Orders' table and a 'Customers' table. The core idea to emphasize is that while 'Customer_ID' exists in both, they are currently like two islands. The Inner Join is the bridge we build between them. I'll narrate this as a quest for 'common ground,' where we only care about rows that have a perfect match on both sides.

To visualize the set logic, I will draw a Venn diagram. This is the most critical visual aid for this session. I’ll shade only the intersection where the two circles overlap. I must explicitly mention that if an order has a Customer_ID that doesn't exist in the Customers table (perhaps a data integrity error) or if a customer has never placed an order, they simply 'disappear' from the results of an Inner Join. This 'exclusion by default' is the most common source of bugs for beginners, so I will pause here to ask the class: 'If we have 100 customers but only 50 have bought something, how many rows will our inner join show?' This forces them to realize the join acts as a filter.

Next, I will transition to the syntax mechanics. On the whiteboard, I'll write out the SELECT statement, color-coding the 'ON' clause. I want to frame the 'ON' keyword not just as syntax, but as the 'matching rule.' I will demonstrate the dot notation (Orders.customer_id = Customers.id) and explain that this is how we tell the database engine exactly which 'bridge' to cross. A common pitfall here is ambiguity—students often forget to specify the table name when column names are identical. I’ll intentionally write a 'broken' query first, let it fail in our mental model, and then fix it by adding the table prefixes to show how we resolve that confusion.

For the first practice task, we will walk through joining 'Orders' and 'Customers.' I will draw a few rows of sample data. I'll pick one order and 'hunt' for its matching customer in the other table. This manual 'lookup' mimics what the database engine does internally (a nested loop join intuition). By showing that the result is a wider table—combining the columns of both—I help them see that JOINs are about horizontal expansion, whereas the later sessions on SET operations will be about vertical stacking.

To wrap up, I will challenge the students with a 'null' scenario. I'll add a row to the 'Orders' table with a NULL customer ID and ask what happens during an Inner Join. This reveals the 'truth' of the Inner Join: it requires a definitive match. Since NULL equals nothing (not even another NULL), that row is discarded. This reinforces the session's goal: Inner Joins are for finding the 'perfect pairs' and ignoring the 'lonely' records on either side.

tasks: Join an 'Orders' table with a 'Customers' table to show the customer name for every order.
Explain the result when a record in the left table has no match in the right table during an inner join.

sessions.title: Left, Right, and Full Outer Joins
sessions.description: This session expands on joins by covering Outer Joins, which allow you to preserve rows even when no match exists in the joined table. You will learn to identify when to use a LEFT JOIN to ensure no data is lost from your primary entity. This is critical for generating comprehensive reports, such as listing all customers even if they haven't placed an order yet.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the 'perfect world' of Inner Joins—where every key has a partner—to the messy reality of real-world data. The core intuition to establish is that data is often incomplete, but incompleteness should not result in invisibility. I will start on the whiteboard by drawing two circles that don't perfectly overlap: a list of 'Customers' and a list of 'Orders.' I’ll ask the class: 'If we use an Inner Join to find who ordered what, what happens to the customer who signed up yesterday but hasn't bought anything yet?' The answer—that they disappear from the result set—sets the stage for the Outer Join as a 'preservation' tool rather than just a 'matching' tool.

Next, I will introduce the LEFT JOIN. The concept-first focus here is the 'Master Table' mental model. I’ll explain that in a LEFT JOIN, the table on the left side of the keyword is treated as the primary entity whose existence we want to guarantee in the output. I will draw a table where a 'Product' exists but the 'Review' column is filled with a large, red 'NULL'. This visual is crucial for correcting the common misconception that NULL means an error; instead, I’ll frame it as a 'meaningful absence.' We’ll walk through the logic: the database attempts to find a match, fails, and instead of discarding the row, it 'pads' the right side with null values. This ensures our product catalog remains intact even if some items are unrated.

To bridge into RIGHT JOINs, I’ll demonstrate that they are functionally mirrors of LEFT JOINs. Rather than teaching them as a brand-new concept, I will frame them as a matter of 'perspective' or 'syntax preference.' I’ll show how 'Customers LEFT JOIN Orders' is identical to 'Orders RIGHT JOIN Customers.' The pedagogical goal here is to discourage students from constantly switching perspectives; I will recommend sticking to LEFT JOINs as a professional standard to keep queries readable from left-to-right, preventing the 'mental gymnastics' of tracking which table is being preserved.

We then move to the FULL OUTER JOIN, which I’ll describe as the 'union of all possibilities.' This is the most complex visualization because it preserves rows from both sides, even if they have no match. I’ll use the example of a merger between two companies: Company A has its list of clients, Company B has its own, and we need a master list showing everyone, identifying who is unique to A, who is unique to B, and who is shared. This highlights the logic of the 'coalesced' view. I will warn students about the performance cost of FULL JOINs, explaining that the database has to do significantly more work to track 'unmatched' rows from both directions.

Finally, we will transition into the practice tasks. I’ll challenge the students to write a query listing all products and their reviews. The 'aha' moment I’m looking for is when they realize that an Inner Join would accidentally hide new products from the store manager’s view. We will conclude by comparing a LEFT and RIGHT join on a specific schema to prove that while the results can be the same, the 'intent' and readability of the code change. This reinforces the idea that SQL is not just about getting the right numbers, but about writing a clear, maintainable contract for data retrieval.

tasks: Write a query to list all products and any associated reviews, including products with no reviews.
Identify the difference in results between a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN for a specific schema.

sessions.title: Self Joins and Cross Joins
sessions.description: This session covers specialized joins: Self Joins for hierarchical data and Cross Joins for Cartesian products. You will learn how to treat a single table as two separate entities to compare rows within the same dataset. This advanced technique is used for tasks like managing employee-manager hierarchies or generating all possible combinations of attributes.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by challenging the assumption that a JOIN always requires two different physical tables. Since we are using a concept-first public lecture style, I will start by drawing a single 'Employees' table on the whiteboard. I'll point out that while every row represents an employee, one column—'manager_id'—actually points to another row within this very same table. This visual realization is the key to unlocking the Self Join. I will explain that the database engine doesn't care if the data comes from the same source; it only cares about the logical relationship. To make this work in SQL, the essential 'trick' is aliasing. I will write the same table name twice on the board but give them different labels, such as 'e' for employee and 'm' for manager, effectively 'cloning' the table in our minds so we can compare rows against one another.

Moving into the mechanics, I will demonstrate the common pitfall where students forget to account for the 'top of the pyramid.' In an organizational chart, the CEO usually has a NULL manager_id. If we use a standard INNER JOIN for a Self Join, the CEO disappears from our results entirely. I will use this moment to bridge back to our previous session on Outer Joins, showing how a LEFT JOIN on a self-referencing table ensures we see the entire hierarchy without losing the leadership. This reinforces the idea that JOIN types are tools we swap out depending on the integrity of the data we want to preserve.

Next, we pivot to the Cross Join, which is the most primitive and 'dangerous' form of joining. I will describe it as the 'blind date' of the database world—every row in Table A meets every row in Table B. Instead of a complex diagram, I'll draw a 3-row table of 'Shirt Colors' and a 4-row table of 'Sizes.' By manually drawing lines connecting every color to every size, I will illustrate the Cartesian Product. The most important takeaway here is the exponential growth of the result set; I’ll explicitly warn that a Cross Join between two tables of 1,000 rows results in 1,000,000 rows. This helps students understand why this join is rarely used by accident in production but is invaluable for generating permutations or test data.

To conclude, we will engage in a mental calculation exercise. I will ask the audience to predict the row count for a Cross Join between an 'Events' table and a 'Venues' table of specific sizes. This isn't just about math; it’s about developing a 'query cost intuition.' We finish by contrasting the two: the Self Join is about finding specific, hidden needles of relationship within a single haystack, while the Cross Join is about building an entirely new, massive haystack from two smaller ones. This distinction ensures they leave the session knowing exactly when to reach for these specialized logical tools.

tasks: Join an 'Employees' table to itself to show the name of each employee's manager.
Calculate the total number of rows produced by a cross join of two tables with specific sizes.

sessions.title: Set Operations: UNION, INTERSECT, EXCEPT
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to combine the results of multiple queries vertically using set theory operations. You will understand the requirements for column compatibility and the difference between UNION and UNION ALL. This provides an alternative way to merge datasets that doesn't rely on specific column relationships, useful for aggregating data from similar but separate tables.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by contrasting what the students have learned about JOINs with the concept of 'Stacking.' While JOINs extend a table horizontally by adding columns from other tables, explain that we often need to merge results vertically. Use the whiteboard to draw two separate lists of users—one from an 'Active' table and one from an 'Archived' table. The core idea here is that these are separate entities that share the same 'shape.' This visualization helps learners understand that Set Operations are not about finding relationships between rows, but about aggregating the rows themselves.

Introduce the strict 'contract' required for Set Operations to work: the columns must match in number and data type compatibility. On the whiteboard, illustrate a common failure point—trying to UNION a table with (Name, ID) with another table that has (ID, Name). Explain that SQL is positional, not name-based, when it comes to sets. This prevents the common misconception that the database will 'figure out' which columns match based on header titles. Use this to reinforce why schema consistency is vital in professional database design.

Dive into the 'UNION' vs. 'UNION ALL' distinction by using a Venn Diagram with overlapping circles. Explain that 'UNION' is computationally more expensive because the database must perform a hidden 'DISTINCT' operation to remove duplicates. In a concept-first public lecture style, frame 'UNION ALL' as the default choice for performance-conscious engineers unless they specifically need to filter out duplicates. Pose a question to the class: 'If I have 1,000 active users and 500 archived users, why might the result of a UNION be 1,450?' This prompts them to realize that some users might exist in both states, and the set operation is what surfaces that data reality.

Transition to the 'Subtraction' logic using the EXCEPT (or MINUS) operator. Use the whiteboard to show a circle of 'New Customers' and then subtract a circle of 'Customers who have Made a Purchase.' This is the most intuitive way to explain finding leads who haven't converted yet. Emphasize that order matters here—unlike UNION, which is commutative, EXCEPT depends entirely on which set is the 'minuend.' This sets up the practice task where students will identify specific customer segments by subtracting one behavior from another.

Conclude by introducing INTERSECT as the search for 'Common Ground.' Re-use the Venn Diagram to highlight only the overlapping center. Explain that while this can often be achieved with an INNER JOIN, INTERSECT is cleaner when the goal is to find identical records across two differently sourced but identically structured datasets. Close the session by summarizing that while JOINs are for building relationships, SET operations are for managing populations. The final practice tasks of combining user lists and filtering new customers will act as the 'litmus test' for whether they understand the vertical vs. horizontal data flow.

tasks: Combine a list of active users and archived users into a single result set.
Use EXCEPT to find customers who are in the 'New' category but have not made a purchase.

lectures.title: Aggregation
lectures.description: This lecture moves from individual rows to data summaries, teaching you how to compute statistics and nest queries for sophisticated analysis.

sessions.title: Aggregate Functions
sessions.description: This session introduces functions like SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, and MAX to perform calculations across multiple rows. You will learn how these functions collapse many rows into a single summary value. This is the basis for all data analytics and business intelligence reporting within a database environment.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting our perspective from looking at rows as individual stories to looking at them as parts of a larger narrative. I will start by drawing a simple spreadsheet on the whiteboard with five rows of 'Orders.' Each row has a price and a quantity. Until now, we’ve learned how to filter or sort these individual events. Now, I’ll ask the central question: 'What is the grand total of our business today?' This marks the transition from data retrieval to data condensation. The core concept here is 'Collapsing': we are taking a vertical stack of data and crushing it down into a single, singular number. I’ll visualize this by drawing arrows from all rows pointing to a single point at the bottom of the table.

I will then introduce the five core 'mathematical eyes' through which we view a dataset: SUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, and MAX. Instead of just listing them, I’ll explain their distinct behaviors using the 'NULL' trap as our primary teaching tool. On the whiteboard, I’ll add a row where the 'Discount' column is empty (NULL). I’ll demonstrate that while COUNT(*) counts the existence of the row, COUNT(discount) might ignore the NULL. This is a critical distinction because it prevents students from providing inaccurate business reports later in their careers. I want them to see these functions not as formulas, but as filters that decide which data points are worthy of being included in the final calculation.

To move into the application phase, we will perform a 'Visual Query' for total revenue. I’ll write the SELECT statement on the board, but I’ll specifically emphasize the syntax: SELECT SUM(price * quantity). This is where many beginners stumble; they often try to sum before they multiply. I’ll use the whiteboard to show that the database performs the horizontal math (price * quantity) for every row first, and then the vertical math (the SUM) at the very end. By showing the 'Horizontal then Vertical' flow, we demystify how complex calculations like revenue are actually computed within the engine.

Finally, we will address the 'Identity Crisis' of an aggregate query. I’ll purposefully write an invalid query on the board: SELECT product_name, MAX(price). I will ask the students: 'If the result is only one row—the maximum price—which product name should the computer show if there are ten different products?' This illustrates why you cannot mix individual row data with aggregate data without specific grouping (which we will cover in the next session). This moment of cognitive dissonance is vital; it teaches them that once you aggregate, the individual identities of the rows are sacrificed for the sake of the summary. We'll conclude by practicing finding the average price and maximum discount, ensuring they understand that multiple aggregations can live in the same SELECT statement, as long as they all share that same 'summarized' soul.

tasks: Calculate the total revenue from an 'Orders' table.
Find the average price and the maximum discount offered across all products.

sessions.title: GROUP BY and HAVING
sessions.description: This session teaches you how to group data into buckets for aggregate calculations and how to filter those buckets using the HAVING clause. You will learn the critical distinction between WHERE (row filter) and HAVING (group filter). Mastering this allows you to answer questions like 'Which categories have an average price over $50?'
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by conceptualizing the database as a physical sorting office. If Session 1 taught us how to count everything on the floor, Session 2 is about sorting items into boxes before we count them. Use a whiteboard to draw a raw list of transactions—messy and varied. Then, visualize the 'GROUP BY' clause as a set of physical buckets. Explain that the database engine takes every row, looks at a specific column (like 'Country' or 'Department'), and tosses the row into the corresponding bucket. This mental model is vital because it explains why every column in your SELECT statement must either be the bucket label itself or an aggregate calculation; you can't see an individual person's name once they've been tossed into a 'Country' bucket.

Transition into the syntax by demonstrating the 'Group-Apply-Combine' strategy. Write a query on the board that counts users per country. Emphasize that the database first groups (sorts into countries), applies the function (counts the rows in each group), and then combines the results into a final summary table. A common pitfall for beginners is trying to select a column that isn't grouped, like 'User_ID' alongside a count of users per country. Address this immediately by asking the class: 'If we have a bucket for the USA containing 500 people, which single User_ID should the database display next to the number 500?' This logic puzzle helps students internalize why non-aggregated columns are illegal in a grouped query.

Introduce the HAVING clause by creating a problem that the WHERE clause cannot solve. Ask the students to find only the countries with more than 50 users. Try to write this using WHERE and then 'fail' intentionally, explaining that WHERE acts like a bouncer at the front door—it filters rows *before* they ever get into the buckets. Since the database doesn't know the count of a group until the grouping is finished, we need a second filter that acts on the buckets themselves. This is HAVING. Draw a timeline on the board: FROM -> WHERE -> GROUP BY -> HAVING -> SELECT. This sequence is the 'holy grail' of SQL execution order and clears up the confusion between row-level filtering and group-level filtering.

Conclude with a practice exercise that forces students to apply both types of filters simultaneously. Ask them to list departments with more than 10 employees, but only counting employees hired after 2020. This task reveals whether they understand the pipeline: first, exclude old employees (WHERE), then organize by department (GROUP BY), and finally, discard small departments (HAVING). By the end of this session, the student should see SQL not as a list of commands, but as a multi-stage processing plant where data is filtered, sorted, and condensed into insights.

tasks: Count the number of users per country.
List departments that have more than 10 employees using GROUP BY and HAVING.

sessions.title: Subqueries
sessions.description: In this session, you will learn to nest one query inside another to perform multi-step data retrieval. You will cover scalar, column, and row subqueries and how they can be used in WHERE or FROM clauses. Subqueries are a powerful tool for dynamic filtering where the filter criteria itself depends on a database lookup.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome students to the concept of 'Inception' for databases: queries within queries. Begin by framing the fundamental limitation of standard SELECT statements—they require you to know the criteria upfront. Ask the audience: 'How do you find employees earning more than the average salary if you don't know the average yet?' This creates the pedagogical 'itch' that subqueries are designed to scratch. Explain that a subquery is simply a temporary calculation used by a main query to make a decision, acting as a bridge between unknown data points and your final result set.

Start the whiteboard session by visualizing the 'Inside-Out' execution flow. Draw a small box representing the Inner Query (the calculation) and a larger box for the Outer Query (the display). The most critical concept here is that the database evaluates the inner query first, replaces it with its resulting value, and then runs the outer query. This 'Evaluation Order' is where most beginners trip up; they try to read SQL from top-to-bottom, but subqueries require us to read from the middle-out. Use the average salary example: first, we calculate the single number (e.g., $60,000), and then we filter the main list for anyone > $60,000.

Introduce the taxonomy of subqueries based on their 'shape.' A Scalar subquery returns a single cell—a single value that can be treated like a constant. Demonstrate how this fits perfectly into a WHERE clause with comparison operators like '=' or '>'. Then, transition to Multi-row subqueries, which return a list. This is the perfect time to introduce the 'IN' operator. Use the analogy of a guest list: the inner query generates the list of VIP IDs, and the outer query checks every person at the door against that list. A common pitfall to mention is trying to use '=' with a multi-row subquery, which will trigger a crash; explain that the database doesn't know which of the many results to compare against, hence the need for 'IN', 'ANY', or 'ALL'.

Shift the focus to the 'Correlated Subquery,' which is often the steepest part of the learning curve. Unlike the previous 'Independent' subqueries that run once and finish, a correlated subquery is 'dependent'—it runs once for every single row in the outer table. Visualize this on the board as a loop. Draw a person row, then show the subquery 'looking back' at that person’s specific department to calculate a local average. This is the difference between 'Is this person's salary above the company average?' (Non-correlated) and 'Is this person's salary above their specific department's average?' (Correlated). Explain that while powerful, correlation can be slow on massive datasets because of this repetitive execution.

Conclude by challenging the students to determine when a subquery is the right tool versus a JOIN. Teach the heuristic that subqueries are excellent for filtering and 'membership' checks, while JOINs are superior for combining data for display. Have them sketch out the logic for finding employees whose department is located in 'New York'—first using a subquery to find NY department IDs, and then considering how a JOIN might achieve the same. This comparison prepares them for the next session on CTEs, where we begin to clean up the often-messy syntax of deeply nested subqueries.

tasks: Find all employees who earn more than the company average salary using a subquery.
Explain the difference between a correlated and non-correlated subquery.

sessions.title: Common Table Expressions
sessions.description: This session introduces Common Table Expressions (CTEs) as a way to create named temporary result sets that improve query readability and maintainability. You will learn how to use the WITH clause to break complex logic into smaller, logical steps. CTEs are the professional standard for writing clean, modular SQL in modern data engineering.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by acknowledging a 'cognitive wall' that many students hit after learning subqueries: the 'Inception' problem. I will draw a messy, multi-level subquery on the board, pointing out how the code grows inward, making it impossible to read top-to-bottom. The core idea of this session is that Common Table Expressions (CTEs) are the 'variables' of the SQL world. I'll frame CTEs not just as a new syntax, but as a mental shift from writing one giant, monolithic instruction to building a pipeline of logical steps. This is crucial because, in professional data engineering, readability is as important as performance.

I will introduce the 'WITH' keyword by visualizing it as a set of named boxes or temporary 'sticky notes' attached to the query. On the whiteboard, I'll show the syntax: 'WITH [Name] AS ( [Logic] )'. The most important takeaway here is that the name we give the CTE becomes a valid table name for the rest of the query. I’ll explain that this 'naming' allows us to treat a complex calculation like a simple table, effectively 'flattening' the nested logic. To make this concrete, I’ll take the average salary subquery from the previous session and refactor it in real-time, showing how the CTE allows us to define 'AverageSalaryTable' at the top before we even get to the 'SELECT' statement.

A common pitfall I will address is the misconception that CTEs are physically stored in the database like permanent tables. I’ll clarify that they only exist for the duration of that single query execution. I will also demonstrate 'chaining'—the ability to define multiple CTEs separated by commas. I’ll draw a flow chart showing data moving from 'RawData' to 'FilteredData' to 'AggregatedData.' This visualization helps learners see SQL as a modular assembly line rather than a single complex math equation. This 'step-by-step' thinking is what separates junior coders from senior engineers.

For the practice phase, we will tackle the 'Monthly Sales Growth' problem. This is a multi-step logic puzzle: first, you must sum daily sales to get a monthly total; then, you must compare that total to the previous month. I’ll guide the students to create the first CTE for the monthly summary. Once they see how easy it is to 'SELECT *' from that CTE to verify their progress, the value of the tool becomes obvious. We will then build the final calculation on top of it. This exercise is designed to reveal that breaking a problem into two simple parts is much easier than trying to solve it in one complex nested block.

tasks: Refactor a complex subquery into a readable CTE.
Use a CTE to calculate monthly sales growth by first summarizing daily sales.
